name: AI in Signal Detection and Its Governance
blurb: Using AI to find new safety signals, and how to govern it.
title: AI in Signal Detection and Its Governance
answer: Beyond case processing, AI helps detect safety signals in large spontaneous report databases and real world data. Published governance work argues these tools should be validated like any GxP system, monitored for data drift and documented so decisions can be explained to regulators.

reading.body:
AI can widen which drug and event pairs reviewers see, but it should not decide what counts as a safety signal. The human assessment and its rationale stay on record.

The pattern here is a division of labour. Statistical methods such as disproportionality analysis flag pairs reported more often than expected, and AI extends that by combining sources like real world data and literature, reading narratives, and prioritising which alerts deserve attention. The decision itself stays with qualified safety experts working through signal management, with regulatory reporting as required.

Governance is the reason this is not just a tooling question. Signal decisions carry regulatory weight, so published work argues these systems should be validated like any GxP system, monitored for data drift as reporting patterns change, and documented so decisions can be explained to regulators. The EMA reflection paper lists signal detection among the uses of AI regulators expect across the medicine lifecycle.

What the data does not cover is performance. It names no accuracy figures, no false positive rates, no comparison against existing statistical methods, and no named vendor systems. It describes an expected governance posture and a division of responsibility, not evidence that AI detects signals better than what pharmacovigilance already uses.

explainer:
A safety signal is information suggesting a new possible link between a medicine and an adverse event, or a new aspect of a known one, that warrants investigation. Signal detection traditionally uses statistical methods on spontaneous report databases, looking for drug and event combinations reported more often than expected.

AI adds the ability to combine many data sources, including real world records and literature, to detect patterns in narratives, and to prioritise which statistical alerts deserve attention. The governance challenge is that signal decisions carry regulatory weight. Tools should be validated, monitored for drift as reporting patterns change, and documented so that the reasoning behind each decision can be explained. The final assessment of whether a signal is real, and what action to take, remains with qualified safety physicians and committees.

What signal detection is

A safety signal is a hint, from reports or data, that a medicine may cause a harm not yet known or known but changing in frequency or severity. Signal detection means scanning adverse event databases, literature, trial data and increasingly real world data for such hints, then assessing whether they are real. The statistical methods, which compare how often a drug and an event appear together against what chance would predict, are decades old and run routinely at companies and regulators.

What AI adds

Machine learning can look at more sources and more combinations than fixed statistical screens, can read free text in case narratives and literature that the structured fields miss, can spot patterns across drugs with similar mechanisms, and can rank candidate signals so assessors spend their time on the ones most likely to matter. Some tools also help with the assessment itself, assembling the evidence for a signal from all available sources into one view. The potential is earlier detection with fewer false alarms.

Why governance matters more here than almost anywhere

A missed signal can mean patients harmed; a false signal can mean a useful medicine restricted. Both are decisions a regulator will examine. So companies document how the model ranks and filters, keep the human assessment of every signal, and record why a candidate signal was closed. They validate the model's detection against known historical signals, test for blind spots in subgroups, and check that it does not quietly suppress signals that fixed methods would have raised. Regulators have made clear that AI may assist signal detection; the decision that something is a signal remains a human one.
